title: Episode 32: The War of the Copper Kings: Clark vs. Daly in Butte
description:
In the late nineteenth century, the mining city of Butte, Montana sat atop the richest copper deposit in the world. Two multi-millionaire mining barons—the flamboyant, vindictive William Andrews Clark and the charismatic, working-class Marcus Daly—waged an all-out personal and political war. They spent fortunes buying state elections with cigars stuffed with thousand-dollar bills, moving the state capital, and fighting subterranean dynamite wars hundreds of feet beneath the earth.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the late nineteenth century, the industrial revolution in America and Europe created an insatiable global thirst for a single reddish metal: copper. As electrical grids, telephone lines, and dynamos wired the modern world, a solitary volcanic mountain in southwestern Montana became known as 'the Richest Hill on Earth.' The mining metropolis of Butte produced a staggering twenty percent of the world's copper supply, generating unprecedented billions in wealth. But that immense wealth became the private battleground for two implacable, ruthless oligarchs: Marcus Daly, the beloved Irish father of the Anaconda Copper Company, and William Andrews Clark, a cold, vanity-obsessed banking tycoon who would stop at nothing to buy a seat in the United States Senate. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE RICHEST HILL ON EARTH
In the late eighteen eighties, Butte, Montana was a roaring, smoky, twenty-four-hour industrial behemoth perched on a mountain slope in the Northern Rockies. Nicknamed 'the Richest Hill on Earth,' its honeycombed granite underground contained the largest, highest-grade veins of copper ore ever discovered. While Butte's surface was a grim, sulfur-choked landscape where smelting fumes stripped the surrounding hills of all vegetation—so thick that streetcars had to run with headlights blazing at noon—its underground was a subterranean empire of tens of thousands of miners and hundreds of blind pit mules working by candlelight thousands of feet below the earth. Controlling this unimaginable treasure were two men of utterly contrasting personalities. Marcus Daly was a warm, charismatic Irish immigrant who had arrived in America penniless at age fifteen. He rose through the mining ranks by sweat and instinct, founding the colossal Anaconda Copper Mining Company. Daly was idolized by his working-class miners because he paid the highest daily wages in the industry, established an eight-hour workday, and drank whiskey with his men in Butte saloons. In sharp contrast stood William Andrews Clark. Clark was a small, fastidious, ice-cold banker and merchant who wore tailored velvet coats, groomed his auburn sideburns with perfumed wax, and counted every single penny. Clark amassed hundreds of millions of dollars in banking, railroads, and mines, but his unquenchable vanity burned with a single, consuming obsession: he wanted to be a United States Senator. In the dark stopes underground, miners toiled in suffocating heat reaching over one hundred and twenty degrees, stripping down to loincloths and pouring ice water over their boots to keep from fainting against the scalding rock faces.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE FEUD IGNITES: THE CAPITAL FIGHT
The personal enmity between Daly and Clark began in eighteen eighty-eight and rapidly escalated into total corporate and political warfare. When Montana achieved statehood in eighteen eighty-nine, Clark ran for territorial delegate to Congress, expecting Daly's endorsement. But Daly, recognizing Clark's utter lack of empathy for the working class, secretly ordered thousands of Anaconda miners to vote for Clark's Republican opponent, defeating him. Clark never forgave the betrayal, swearing to spend every dollar of his vast fortune to ruin Daly. The rivalry exploded onto the statewide stage in eighteen ninety-four during the bitter referendum to determine Montana's permanent state capital. Clark poured hundreds of thousands of dollars into promoting the city of Helena, while Daly spent an estimated two million dollars backing the town of Anaconda, where his giant smelting works operated. It was the most corrupt election in frontier history: Clark's agents handed out free cigars wrapped in twenty-dollar bills, paid off newspapers across the state, and bought entire voter rolls. When the ballots were counted, Helena won by a razor-thin margin of less than two thousand votes. Clark threw a victory banquet in Helena, spending thirty thousand dollars on champagne and boasting that he had defeated Daly's empire. Saloons across the state poured free bourbon, and brass bands marched down main streets day and night, as both tycoons sought to purchase the electoral soul of Montana with rivers of silver and gold.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: CLARK BUYS THE UNITED STATES SENATE
Clark's supreme ambition remained the United States Senate. In the eighteen nineties, before the Seventeenth Amendment established the direct election of senators by popular vote, senators were chosen by state legislatures. In January eighteen ninety-nine, the Montana State Legislature convened in Helena to select the state's new senator. Clark arrived in Helena with a retinue of private bankers and trunks filled with cash. Clark's agents set up private suites in the Helena Hotel, summoning state legislators for late-night conferences. Lawmakers walked in as impoverished ranchers and walked out with envelopes containing between five thousand and twenty thousand dollars in cash—stuffed into hollowed-out cigars and whiskey bottles. One state senator, Fred Whiteside, took the bribes to a legislative committee, producing thirty thousand dollars in crisp one-thousand-dollar bills on the Senate floor as proof of Clark's brazen bribery. Yet Clark was undaunted: he simply increased his payments, spending a staggering one hundred and forty thousand dollars in forty-eight hours. When the final roll call was taken, forty-seven of the ninety-three legislators voted to send William Andrews Clark to the United States Senate. Mark Twain famously remarked of Clark: 'He is as clean a man as one could wish, externally; his makeup is whole and neat. But he has bought a legislature, and sent it to Washington, as casually as one would buy a dog.' The scandal rocked the nation, leading newspaper cartoonists in New York and Chicago to depict Montana as an auction house where the United States Senate was sold to the highest bidder like a prized thoroughbred horse.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: DALY'S REVENGE IN WASHINGTON
Marcus Daly was not a man to accept defeat lying down. Armed with sworn affidavits, hotel registers, and the unspent bribe money produced on the Montana Senate floor, Daly dispatched a team of high-powered attorneys and private investigators to Washington, D.C. In early nineteen hundred, the United States Senate Committee on Privileges and Elections launched a massive federal investigation into Clark's election. For three months, sensational daily hearings exposed the shocking details of Montana's bribery circus, making Clark the laughingstock of the nation. Facing a unanimous committee recommendation for his expulsion from the Senate, Clark was forced to resign in disgrace on May fifteenth, nineteen hundred. But Clark had prepared an audacious constitutional trick. Clark's political ally, Montana's Lieutenant Governor A.E. Spriggs, waited until Governor Robert Smith—a Daly loyalist—briefly left the state on an out-of-state trip. The moment Smith crossed the state line, Spriggs assumed acting governor powers and instantly signed an official executive order re-appointing William Andrews Clark to the very Senate seat he had just resigned! When Governor Smith rushed back to Helena and revoked the appointment, Clark was denied his seat, but his brazen audacity stunned the entire nation. Even in defeat, Clark took pride in outmaneuvering his enemies, boasting to intimate friends that money was the only universal language that never suffered from mistranslation in politics.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SUBTERRANEAN DYNAMITE WARS
While the political wars raged in Washington, the conflict turned physical and deadly hundreds of feet beneath the streets of Butte. Following Marcus Daly's death in late nineteen hundred, a flamboyant young Harvard-educated promoter named F. Augustus Heinze joined the fray, launching the 'subterranean war.' Under the federal Apex Law of eighteen seventy-two, a mining company had the legal right to follow any vein of ore wherever it plunged underground, provided the vein apexed on their surface claim. Claiming that Anaconda veins apexed on his tiny sliver of ground, Heinze and Clark's crews tunneled directly into Anaconda mine stopes. Down in the dark, three thousand feet below the surface, miners fought pitched battles in the drifts. Crews turned high-pressure fire hoses of scalding mine water on one another, dropped sticks of dynamite down ventilation pipes, and blew burning sulfur and pepper through air hoses to smoke rival crews out of the stopes. Underground miners worked with revolvers belted over their overalls, and dozens of miners were injured in subterranean ambushes before federal courts finally intervened to issue injunctions and settle boundary lines. The underground war became so intense that shifts of miners refused to descend into the shafts without armed guards and crates of repeating rifles stacked beside the ore hoisting cages.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE END OF AN ERA IN BUTTE
The War of the Copper Kings finally drew to a close in the early twentieth century. Clark finally won a legitimate term in the United States Senate in nineteen oh-one, serving six quiet, unremarkable years before retiring to pursue European art collecting. When Clark died in nineteen twenty-five at the age of eighty-six, his estate was valued at over two hundred million dollars—equivalent to billions today—including an eighty-four-room palace on Fifth Avenue in New York City with four art galleries, twenty-six bedrooms, and a private Turkish bath. Meanwhile, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was acquired by the Standard Oil trust, which unified Butte's mines under corporate monopoly, paving the way for the open-pit mining of the Berkeley Pit decades later. Butte slowly transitioned from a wild, democratic union stronghold into a tightly controlled company town, where Anaconda Copper owned every newspaper, hotel, and bank in the state.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BIRTH OF THE SEVENTEENTH AMENDMENT
Beyond the dramatic personalities of Clark and Daly, the War of the Copper Kings left a permanent, revolutionary imprint on the American Constitution. The national outrage ignited by Clark's brazen bribery of the Montana State Legislature became the primary catalyst that pushed the United States Congress to reform the Senate. For decades, the Senate had been widely condemned by the public as the 'Millionaires' Club,' where wealthy industrialists, rail barons, and mining magnates bought state legislatures to secure Senate seats with zero accountability to voters. Armed with evidence from the Montana investigations, progressive reformers led by William Jennings Bryan and Robert La Follette campaigned tirelessly for direct popular election. In nineteen thirteen, their efforts culminated in the ratification of the Seventeenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, forever stripping corrupt state legislatures of the power to choose senators and placing the ballot directly into the hands of the American people. The copper barons of Butte had sought to buy an empire, but in their corruption, they inadvertently delivered a major triumph for American democracy.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The War of the Copper Kings was a colossal spectacle of greed, ambition, and power that shaped modern America. It proved that while mountains of copper can buy empires and politicians, the democratic will of the people will ultimately prevail. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we explore the masked vigilantes of Alder Gulch and the mysterious code 3-7-77. Until then, stay curious.
